explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, the sound came "from heaven" (Acts 2:2). Not from the street, not from a neighbor's window. Then it filled the whole house where they were sitting. I've heard a drawer slam shut over my head, but nothing like that.

The Mount of Olives is a fair guess, but the text says the sound came "from heaven" (Acts 2:2). It also says it filled the whole house where they were sitting. Nobody had to go looking for it, because it came to them.

The temple courts are a busy place, so I see why you'd pick them. But Acts 2:2 says the sound came "from heaven," and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. That means the sound came to the people in the house. They didn't have to go looking for it.

That's right, baker. They saw "…tongues like flames of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them." (Acts 2:3). Each of them, every single one. I stand next to an oven all day and I've never once had a flame show up and sit politely on my hat.

This one is true, friend. Acts 2:3 says, "They saw tongues like flames of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them." Notice it says "like" flames of fire. Each person got one, so nobody was skipped.

Yes! "…they were all filled with the Holy Spirit…" (Acts 2:4). All of them, not just a few. The Spirit is what filled them, plain and simple. And right after that, they began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.

Yes, friend, "…each one heard them speaking his own language." (Acts 2:6). That's why the crowd came together in bewilderment. Picture each person in that crowd hearing their own language.

A name is a fun guess, but that's not what the text says. It says each one heard them speaking "…his own language." (Acts 2:6). That's what left the crowd bewildered. Hearing your own name is nice, but hearing your own language is something else.

Close to the subject, but not the word. Acts 2:6 says that when the sound rang out, a crowd came together in bewilderment, because each one heard them speaking "…his own language." The text doesn't say what kind of words they heard until later, in verse 11.

That's it, baker. The crowd asks, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans?" (Acts 2:7). Galileans, folks from the region of Galilee. They're asking how people from one place could be speaking so many languages. I wouldn't know either, and I only speak Cookie.

Samaria is a real region, but it isn't the one the crowd names. They ask, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans?" (Acts 2:7). So they're from Galilee. The crowd is amazed because of where these speakers come from.
Bethany is a fair guess, but the crowd says, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans?" (Acts 2:7). Galileans means people from Galilee. That's the detail that has the crowd so astounded.

Yes, friend! The crowd says, "…we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!" (Acts 2:11). So the topic wasn't small talk. It was the wonders of God, and every listener heard it in their own tongue.

Not quite, baker. Acts 2:12 says they were "Astounded and perplexed…" and they asked one another, "What does this mean?" That's a group still asking what it all means.

Right, they didn't get it right away. The crowd was "Astounded and perplexed…" and they asked one another, "What does this mean?" (Acts 2:12). Hearing something amazing and understanding it are two different things. I once stared at a mixer manual for a week, so I know that feeling.

explanations.answer: They are drunk on new wine
explanations.explanation: That's what they said. The mockers said, "They are drunk on new wine!" (Acts 2:13). That was one reaction in the crowd, because others were asking what it all meant. This story isn't finished, so stay with me.

That's a sensible guess for what a mocker might say, but it isn't what the text has. The mockers said, "They are drunk on new wine!" (Acts 2:13). They had a very specific accusation. The text doesn't say any more about it here.
